I have gathered substantial material from the searches and fetches. Let me now compile the verse-by-verse commentary notes using what I found. Here are my findings:

---

## Esther 1: Verse-by-Verse Commentary Notes

### v. 1 — "This is what happened in the days of Xerxes, who reigned over 127 provinces from India to Cush."

- **Ahasuerus is the historical Xerxes I** (reigned 486–465 BC). The Hebrew name "Akhashverosh" matches the Persian "Khshayarsha," rendered "Xerxes" in Greek. — Ellicott (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/esther/1.htm)
- **Gill** notes that, of the three men called "Ahasuerus" in the OT, this one fits Xerxes best. He inherited the empire from his father Darius I (Hystaspis) and reigned at least 12 years (see Esther 3:7). — Gill (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/esther/1.htm)
- **David Guzik (Enduring Word)** notes that this vast empire covered modern-day Turkey, Iraq, Iran, Pakistan, Jordan, Lebanon, Israel, and parts of Egypt, Sudan, Libya, and Arabia — the largest the world had yet seen. — Enduring Word (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/esther-1/)
- **Ellicott** adds that the 127 provinces were subdivisions of the larger satrapies (Herodotus lists only about 20–29 satrapies). Ethiopia (Cush) paid tribute to Xerxes according to Herodotus. — Ellicott (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/esther/1.htm)

---

### v. 2 — "In those days King Xerxes sat on his royal throne in the citadel of Susa."

- **Shushan (Susa)** was the winter capital of the Persian kings, also mentioned in Nehemiah 1:1. — Gill (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/esther/1.htm), Ellicott (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/esther/1.htm)
- **Gill** notes Xerxes was "settled" on his throne after subduing Egypt in his second year and enjoying peace. — Gill (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/esther/1.htm)
- **Guzik** adds that archaeologists have discovered the ruins of this very palace. — Enduring Word (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/esther-1/)
- **Historical context (Guzik):** At this time (approx. 483 BC), Xerxes was planning his doomed invasion of Greece. Athens was in its classical glory; Ezra had returned to Jerusalem; the rebuilt temple was about 30 years old. — Enduring Word (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/esther-1/)
- **Ellicott** dates the great feast to 483 BC, when Xerxes held a council of princes at Susa to plan the Greek invasion. — Ellicott (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/esther/1.htm)

---

### v. 3 — "In the third year of his reign, Xerxes held a feast for all his officials and servants…"

- **Ellicott** connects this to the historical meeting of nobles to plan the Greek campaign. Rejoicing for a recently concluded successful war in Egypt may have mingled with hopes for the coming invasion. — Ellicott (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/esther/1.htm)
- **Gill** notes it was Persian custom to debate important affairs at banquets, so this feast may have had a political purpose — securing support for the Greek war. — Gill (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/esther/1.htm)
- **The Pulpit Commentary (Homiletics)** calls the motive "vanity — a childish love of display, a vainglorious desire to witness the effect of the splendours of his person and palace on the magnates of his empire." — Pulpit Commentary (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/homiletics/esther/1.htm)
- **The Hebrew word *partemim* ("nobles")** is a Persian loan-word literally meaning "first," related to the Greek *protos* and Latin *primus*. — Ellicott (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/esther/1.htm)

---

### v. 4 — "And for a full 180 days he displayed the glorious riches of his kingdom and the magnificent splendor of his greatness."

- **Guzik:** The first feast (for government officials) lasted 180 days. The basic reason was pride — impressing subjects with wealth, power, majesty, and generosity — a pattern typical of Gentile rulers who "lord it over them" (cf. Matthew 20:25). He likely paid for it from the public treasury. — Enduring Word (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/esther-1/)
- **Gill** cites Daniel 11:2, that Xerxes was "far richer than all" previous Persian kings, and notes a Chinese emperor once held a feast lasting 120 days. He suggests the same guests did not stay the whole 180 days — companies rotated successively. — Gill (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/esther/1.htm)
- **Ellicott** finds half a year of mere feasting "simply incredible" and argues the 180 days included time for mustering troops and planning the invasion. — Ellicott (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/esther/1.htm)
- **Pulpit Commentary:** "His mind was puffed up by the conceit of his high-mightiness; he thirsted for the admiring homage of the world — not an homage attracted by mental greatness or moral worth… but that low and degrading homage which fawns and flatters in presence of the vulgar ostentations of material pomp and power." — Pulpit Commentary (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/homiletics/esther/1.htm)

---

### v. 5 — "…the king held a seven-day feast for all the people in the citadel of Susa, from the least to the greatest."

- **Guzik:** The second feast was for the citizens of the capital, lasting seven days. — Enduring Word (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/esther-1/)
- **Gill** notes the garden court must have been very large to accommodate all who came; he cites a Persian king who once supped with 15,000 men and spent 40 talents on the meal. — Gill (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/esther/1.htm)
- **Ellicott** compares this to Cyrus feasting "all the Persians" (Herodotus i.126). — Ellicott (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/esther/1.htm)
- **Gill** also notes a Jewish tradition (Midrash) claiming the guests were all Jews, numbering 18,500 — but he calls this "not probable." — Gill (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/esther/1.htm)

---

### v. 6 — "Hangings of white and blue linen… silver rings on marble pillars… gold and silver couches… mosaic pavement…"

- **Ellicott** explains that "white and blue (or violet) were the royal colours of Persia." The Hebrew *carpas* means "cotton" (not "green" as the KJV has it). The "beds" are reclining couches, with gold and silver referring to the framework, not merely coverings. — Ellicott (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/esther/1.htm)
- **Gill** provides extensive detail: "carpas" may be Carpasian linen; the cords were purple linen fastened to silver rings on pillars; the couches were of lambs' wool with gold posts and silver feet. The pavement included porphyry, Parian, alabaster, and variously coloured marble. He notes some interpret the stones as precious gems — e.g., the Talmud describes one stone (*dar*) that if placed in a dining room gives light like noonday. — Gill (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/esther/1.htm)
- **Guzik (jokingly):** The Hebrew describes the white hangings as literally "white stuff" — "This may be evidence that Esther was written with a man's eye for decorating detail, not a woman's." — Enduring Word (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/esther-1/)

---

### v. 7 — "Beverages were served in an array of goblets of gold, each with a different design, and the royal wine flowed freely, according to the king's bounty."

- **Ellicott** notes the "royal wine" in Hebrew implies more than wine from royal cellars — possibly wine of Helbon (Ezekiel 27:18), famous in antiquity. The phrase "according to the state of the king" is literally "according to the hand of the king." — Ellicott (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/esther/1.htm)
- **Gill** says the diversity of vessels (same metal, different designs) "made the festival the more grand." He notes that among Persians, earthen cups were considered very mean — a king would disgrace a man by making him use them. — Gill (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/esther/1.htm)
- **Gill** also addresses a Targum tradition: these were the golden vessels of Solomon's Temple taken by Nebuchadnezzar. He rejects this because Cyrus had already returned them to Zerubbabel (Ezra 1:7). — Gill (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/esther/1.htm)

---

### v. 8 — "By order of the king, no limit was placed on the drinking, and every official of his household was to serve each man whatever he desired."

- **Ellicott** explains that "according to the law" means a special ordinance for this occasion: the king commanded that each man drink as he pleased, rather than being compelled — as was the degrading custom in Persian banquets where guests were forced to drink. He notes the Persians were originally a temperate people but had degenerated. — Ellicott (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/esther/1.htm)
- **Gill** cites Xenophon: formerly Persians did not bring large vessels to feasts, but later "they drink so much, that they themselves must be carried out, because they cannot go upright." The Greeks had a custom: "either a man must drink or go out." Ahasuerus forbade compulsion. — Gill (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/esther/1.htm)
- **Guzik:** "Among some of the ancients, each guest was obliged to have a drink with the current round, or else leave the party." — Enduring Word (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/esther-1/)

---

### v. 9 — "Queen Vashti also gave a banquet for the women in the royal palace of King Xerxes."

- **Gill:** It was not customary among Persians or other Eastern nations to admit women to festivals; women feasted separately. Vashti's feast was inside the palace, which was more decent than the open garden where men might see them. — Gill (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/esther/1.htm)
- **Ellicott** notes the name Vashti (per Gesenius) means "beautiful." The Greek writers name Xerxes' queen as Amestris, "of whose cruelty and dissolute life numerous details are given us by Herodotus." Ellicott rejects identifying Esther with Amestris and notes possible theories: Vashti = Amestris (the names being different reproductions of Persian, or Vashti being a title) with a *temporary* deposition, or Amestris was a wife who had influence between Vashti's fall and Esther's rise. — Ellicott (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/esther/1.htm)
- **Guzik:** This was the third of three feasts mentioned. — Enduring Word (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/esther-1/)

---

### v. 10 — "On the seventh day, when the king's heart was merry with wine, he ordered the seven eunuchs who served him—Mehuman, Biztha, Harbona, Bigtha, Abagtha, Zethar, and Carkas—"

- **The clear implication (Guzik):** Ahasuerus was drunk. — Enduring Word (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/esther-1/)
- **Gill:** Jewish tradition says this was the Sabbath day. The king "was intoxicated with it, and knew not well what he said or did." — Gill (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/esther/1.htm)
- **Baptist perspective (Garner-Howes Baptist Commentary):** "His debauched mind conceived of a plan to parade his beautiful queen before his dissipated courtiers, something he might not have done in his sober moments. This goes to illustrate the power of intoxication over the mind of those who indulge in it (Ephesians 5:18)." — Garner-Howes (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ghb/esther-1.html)
- **The seven chamberlains** are eunuchs — appropriate for being sent to the queen, as eunuchs waited upon women in Eastern courts. — Gill (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/esther/1.htm)

---

### v. 11 — "to bring Queen Vashti before him, wearing her royal crown, to display her beauty to the people and officials. For she was beautiful to behold."

- **Guzik:** It is not specifically said, but the implication is that Vashti was expected to display herself in an **immodest** way. Jewish tradition says the request arose from an argument among the drunken men as to which country had the most beautiful women — Xerxes decided to settle it by putting his wife on public display. — Enduring Word (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/esther-1/)
- **Gill** says bringing her "with the crown royal" was to make her "look the more grand and majestic," but he comments: "which was not wisely done, neither was it comely nor safe." — Gill (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/esther/1/)
- **Reformed perspective (Ligonier):** Xerxes called for Vashti "likely to encourage patriotic fervor" at this pre-war banquet. — Ligonier (https://learn.ligonier.org/devotionals/trouble-in-persian-court)

---

### v. 12 — "Queen Vashti, however, refused to come at the king's command brought by his eunuchs. And the king became furious, and his anger burned within him."

- **Guzik (Pentecostal/Charismatic):** Vashti's refusal was "not a sin of rebellion but an act of wisdom and modesty." She had enough moral sense to know this was something she should not do. Wives must submit to husbands (Ephesians 5:22), but that submission "is always conditioned by the higher obligation to obey God before man — a wife may disobey without sinning, but she should do so with a submissive and respectful attitude." — Enduring Word (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/esther-1/)
- **Guzik quotes Adam Clarke:** "What woman, possessing even a common share of prudence and modesty, could consent to expose herself to the view of such a group of drunken Bacchanalians? Her courage was equal to her modesty… Hail, noble woman! Be thou a pattern to all thy sex on every similar occasion!" — Enduring Word (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/esther-1/)
- **Gill:** Vashti may have refused not from pride, but because she concluded the king was drunk and didn't know what he was doing — had she come, he might later blame her. Also, contrary to Persian law, women were not to be seen by strangers. — Gill (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/esther/1.htm)
- **Spurgeon (Baptist):** Ahasuerus was "so far gone with wine as to forget all the proprieties of eastern life," and Vashti was "evidently a woman of right royal spirit" who "refused to degrade herself by being made a spectacle before that ribald rout of drinking princes." — Spurgeon (https://www.spurgeon.org/sermons/providence-as-seen-in-the-book-of-esther)
- **Reformed (Ligonier):** This episode would have caused Jews to wonder: "Is he really so mighty? He cannot even control his own household. Perhaps he is not so terrifying after all." The detailed account serves to show "as mighty as the rulers of this world may seem, they are not finally in control. Only God is sovereign over all." — Ligonier (https://learn.ligonier.org/devotionals/trouble-in-persian-court)
- **Guzik also notes a Jewish tradition** (which he calls "obviously fanciful"): Vashti was ready to appear naked, but God smote her with leprosy just as she received the request. — Enduring Word (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/esther-1/)

---

### vv. 13–14 — "Then the king consulted the wise men who knew the times…"

- **Gill** notes the "wise men" were those skilled in astronomy/astrology ("who understood the times") as well as law and justice — the king's customary counselors. — Gill (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/esther/1.htm)
- **Guzik:** The seven princes named had "personal access to the king and ranked highest in the kingdom." — Enduring Word (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/esther-1/)

---

### vv. 15–18 — "According to law, what should be done with Queen Vashti…?" Memucan's reply.

- **Guzik:** Memucan's argument was that Vashti's conduct would become known to all women throughout the empire, causing them to "despise their husbands." The fear was that "this very day the noble ladies of Persia and Media" who had heard of Vashti's conduct would say the same thing to their husbands. — Enduring Word (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/esther-1/)
- **Garner-Howes Baptist Commentary:** "One of the counselors, Memucan, had an answer. He reasoned that Vashti's disobedience was not harmful to the king only, but to all the men of the empire as well. The refusal of the queen to obey the king would become known widely… and all the wives of the realm would conclude that they could disobey their husbands also." — Garner-Howes (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ghb/esther-1.html)
- **GotQuestions (Evangelical):** Memucan argued that "such a bad example as Queen Vashti had set must be dealt with harshly." — GotQuestions (https://www.gotquestions.org/Vashti-Xerxes.html) *(from search excerpt)*

---

### v. 19 — "…let him issue a royal decree… recorded in the laws of Persia and Media so that it cannot be repealed, that Vashti shall never again enter the presence of King Xerxes…"

- **The irrevocability of Persian law** was a well-known constitutional feature. — Ellicott (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/esther/1.htm)
- **Guzik:** This was harsh and foolish — Xerxes "should have honored the dignity of his queen." History's profile of Xerxes shows him as an unreasonable and foolish man (e.g., he once executed bridge-builders because a storm destroyed their bridge, then commanded the sea to be whipped and chained). — Enduring Word (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/esther-1/)

---

### vv. 20–22 — The edict proclaimed: "all women… will honor their husbands" / "every man should be master of his own household."

- **Guzik:** The goal was admirable — reinforcing a husband's honor in the home — but the means were foolish. "A man cannot demand or coerce respect from his wife — if it isn't freely given, then it isn't worth anything." He notes Paul's instruction: "let the wife see that she respects her husband" (Ephesians 5:33). — Enduring Word (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/esther-1/)
- **Garner-Howes Baptist Commentary takes a notably different tone:** "While the law of Ahasuerus was provoked by the refusal of a sinful demand, it was, nevertheless, according to God's intent as set forth in the beginning (Genesis 3:16) and in keeping with New Testament instruction (Ephesians 5:22-24)." The commentary lists as a lesson: "God's wise law has decreed that the wife should be subject to her husband." — Garner-Howes (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ghb/esther-1.html)
- **Smith's Bible Commentary:** Notes the cultural context — "Women were actually considered just one step above a slave. They had very little rights." When Vashti refused, the men feared: "when we get home and our wives hear that your wife refused to come in at your command, we're not going to be able to handle the women." — Smith (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/csc/esther-1.html) *(from search excerpt)*
- **Guzik** also notes the decree was sent "to each province in its own script and to each people in their own language," showing the empire's vast diversity. — Enduring Word (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/esther-1/)
- **Gill** interprets the final phrase about every man being "master in his own house" as meaning "prince, lord, and master there, and his commands obeyed, not only by his children and servants, but by his wife also." — Gill (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/esther/1-22.htm) *(from search excerpt)*

---

## Key Points of Comparison Across Traditions

### Vashti: heroine or rebel?

| Tradition | View of Vashti |
|---|---|
| **Pentecostal/Charismatic (Guzik/Enduring Word)** | Vashti acted with "wisdom and modesty"; her refusal was not sinful rebellion. Wives submit to husbands but must obey God first. |
| **Baptist (Spurgeon)** | Vashti was "a woman of right royal spirit" who refused to degrade herself. The king was at fault for his drunken, immodest demand. |
| **Baptist (Garner-Howes)** | Vashti's refusal "humiliated the king." While the king's demand was "sinful," the resulting decree was still "according to God's intent" (Gen 3:16) and consistent with NT teaching on wifely submission. |
| **Reformed (Ligonier)** | The episode is read providentially: it shows the king's weakness (he can't even control his own household), teaching that earthly rulers are not ultimately in control — only God is. |

### The 180-day feast: what was it?

| View | Interpretation |
|---|---|
| **Traditional (Guzik, Gill)** | Rotating groups of officials were feasted over a 180-day period — a display of pride and wealth. |
| **Anglican scholarly (Ellicott)** | The 180 days included mustering troops and planning the Greek invasion; a half-year of mere feasting is "simply incredible." |
| **Pulpit Commentary (Homiletics)** | Motivated by "vanity — a childish love of display" and "vainglorious" pride. |

### The purpose of the detailed description

| View | Emphasis |
|---|---|
| **Reformed (Ligonier)** | The lavish detail highlights Persian power so that the reader sees through it: "only God is sovereign over all." |
| **Pentecostal/Charismatic (Guzik)** | The description exposes the pride and folly of worldly rulers (cf. Matt 20:25) and sets up the providential chain of events leading to Esther's elevation. |
| **All traditions (Spurgeon, Precept Austin, Pulpit Commentary)** | The book, though God's name never appears, is "a veritable treatise on the doctrine of Divine Providence." — Precept Austin (https://www.preceptaustin.org/esther_1-2_commentary); Spurgeon (https://www.spurgeon.org/sermons/providence-as-seen-in-the-book-of-esther) |
